```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 6, out.width = "100%")
library(hypergraphs)
join_and <- function(v) sub(", ([^,]*)$", " and \\1", toString(v))
ordinal <- function(k) {
  k <- as.integer(k)
  suffix <- if (k %% 100L %in% 11:13) "th" else
    c("th", "st", "nd", "rd", rep("th", 6L))[k %% 10L + 1L]
  sprintf("%d%s", k, suffix)
}
```

A text hypergraph is defined by both its node types and the relation
represented by a hyperedge. A document can link its words, a word can link
the documents containing it, and a sentence or token window can link words
within a smaller textual unit. An alternative uses document embeddings
to define groups of nearby documents. These constructions encode different
relations and can therefore produce different measures and partitions.

This tutorial compares the four constructions available through
`text_hypergraph()`: `"bag"`, `"window"`, `"sentence"`, and `"knn"`.
Three short documents first illustrate their memberships. A corpus of
`r nrow(covid_abstracts)` abstracts then shows how the representation
affects word centrality and document clustering.

## Three documents

The three documents share several terms. Removing the common words
listed by `stop_words_en()` makes their retained memberships easier to
inspect. This preprocessing is applied before the hyperedges are formed.

```{r docs}
docs <- c(
  online   = "Students learn online. Teachers prepare online lessons.",
  assess   = "Teachers assess students. Online assessment needs feedback.",
  distance = "Distance learning needs feedback. Students value feedback."
)
stops <- stop_words_en()
```

### Bag of words

The bag-of-words construction discards word order and records word
counts within documents. With `nodes = "word"`, words are nodes and each
document is a hyperedge containing its retained words. This orientation
is used for document-level word hypergraphs such as those considered by
Ding et al. (2020).

```{r bag-word}
bag_word <- text_hypergraph(docs, nodes = "word", stop_words = stops)
bag_word
```

```{r bag-word-values, include = FALSE}
toy_vocab <- hg_get(bag_word, what = "vocabulary")
in_all <- subset(toy_vocab, doc_freq == length(docs))$word
in_two <- subset(toy_vocab, doc_freq == 2)$word
```

Each enclosed region represents the retained words of one document.

```{r bag-word-plot, fig.alt = "Three documents plotted as hyperedges over their words"}
plot(bag_word)
```

The regions overlap at shared words. `r join_and(in_all)` occurs in
all three documents, and `r join_and(in_two)` occurs in two. Each remaining
word belongs to one document. The figure displays membership, while the
incidence weights retain repeated word counts.

With `nodes = "doc"`, documents become nodes and each word becomes a
hyperedge containing its documents. This orientation is used for document
clustering and classification (Hayashi et al. 2020). Its weighted incidence
matrix is the transpose of the word-oriented matrix. The two hypergraphs
are therefore dual representations (Berge 1989), and `dual_hypergraph()`
converts between them.

```{r bag-doc}
bag_doc <- text_hypergraph(docs, stop_words = stops)
dual_hypergraph(bag_doc)
```

The dual has `r nrow(toy_vocab)` word nodes and
`r length(docs)` document hyperedges. Its incidence matches `bag_word`,
which was constructed directly in that orientation.

The default incidence weight is a within-document count. With
`weight = "tfidf"`, that count is multiplied by the smoothed inverse
document frequency `log((1 + N) / (1 + df)) + 1`, where `N` is the number
of retained documents and `df` is the number containing the word. A word
in every document has multiplier one; less widely distributed words have
larger multipliers. This convention should be stated when comparing
tf-idf representations across software.

```{r tfidf}
bag_tfidf <- text_hypergraph(docs, nodes = "word", weight = "tfidf",
                             stop_words = stops)
hg_get(bag_tfidf, what = "vocabulary")
```

```{r tfidf-values, include = FALSE}
tfidf_vocab <- hg_get(bag_tfidf, what = "vocabulary")
idf_all <- unique(round(subset(tfidf_vocab, doc_freq == 3)$idf, 2))
idf_one <- unique(round(subset(tfidf_vocab, doc_freq == 1)$idf, 2))
```

For this corpus, the inverse-document-frequency multiplier is
`r idf_all` for a word in all three documents and `r idf_one` for a word
in one document. The vocabulary table reports the counts, document
frequencies, and multipliers used in the construction.

### Windows of words

The window construction forms a hyperedge from the distinct words in
each run of consecutive retained tokens. Window positions remain within
individual documents. Sliding windows advance by one token; tumbling
windows advance by the window length and can include a shorter final
segment. Identical member sets are combined. Their incidence weights
summarise how often the retained set occurs across windows.
This defines local co-occurrence after preprocessing, rather than
preserving the complete sequence within a hyperedge.

```{r window}
tumbling <- text_hypergraph(docs, construction = "window", window = 3,
                            window_mode = "tumbling", stop_words = stops)
tumbling
```

```{r window-values, include = FALSE}
sliding <- text_hypergraph(docs, construction = "window", window = 3,
                           stop_words = stops)
n_sliding <- length(unique(hg_get(sliding)$edge))
n_tumbling <- length(unique(hg_get(tumbling)$edge))
```

The plot displays each distinct window set as an enclosed region and
shows its frequency.

```{r window-plot, fig.alt = "Tumbling windows of three words plotted as hyperedges"}
plot(tumbling)
```

After stop-word removal, each document contains seven tokens. With
tumbling windows of length three, it contributes two full windows and one
single-token segment. The last segments of the second and third documents
both contain `feedback` and are combined with count two. The word `lessons`
has no other word in its segment. Sliding windows produce
`r n_sliding` distinct sets, compared with `r n_tumbling` for tumbling
windows. The difference reflects the change in window positions.

### Sentences

The sentence construction creates one hyperedge per nonempty sentence
segment. This implementation splits text at `.`, `!`, `?`, and `;`, then
records within-segment word counts. It is a punctuation-based
approximation to sentence boundaries, so abbreviations and other special
cases may require preprocessing. Sentence hypergraphs are one of the
constructions used by Ding et al. (2020).

```{r sentence}
sentences <- text_hypergraph(docs, construction = "sentence",
                             stop_words = stops)
hg_get(sentences, what = "sentences")
```

The sentence table identifies each segment's document, position, and
retained token count. Inspecting it helps verify that the segmentation
matches the intended textual units.

```{r sentence-plot, fig.alt = "Six sentences plotted as hyperedges over their words"}
plot(sentences)
```

The example produces six sentence segments. `teachers` and `prepare`
share a segment, whereas `teachers` and `feedback` share a document but
not a segment. The sentence construction therefore imposes a more local
co-occurrence relation than the bag-of-words construction.

### Nearest neighbours in an embedding space

The k-nearest-neighbour construction uses document embeddings as its
input. It forms one hyperedge per document, containing that document and
its `k` nearest neighbours by cosine similarity. The resulting relations
depend on the encoder and neighbourhood size; cosine proximity is an
operational measure of similarity, not a direct measurement of meaning.
Feature-based hyperedge construction is also used in hypergraph neural
networks (Feng et al. 2019). The corpus below provides precomputed embeddings.

## The corpus

`covid_abstracts` contains `r nrow(covid_abstracts)` research abstracts
about COVID-19 and education. `covid_embeddings` contains their aligned
`all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeddings, with `r ncol(covid_embeddings)` coordinates
per abstract. The document identifiers must align when embeddings are
supplied to the constructor.

Vocabulary filtering changes both membership and incidence weights.
`stop_words` removes specified terms, `min_count` sets a corpus-frequency
threshold, and `min_chars` sets a minimum token length. `max_words` caps
vocabulary size; `coverage` selects frequent words until a specified share
of tokens is represented. The following example uses a common stop list,
`min_count = 3`, and `min_chars = 3` for the token-based constructions.

```{r corpus-vocabulary}
stops <- c(stop_words_en(), "using", "used", "use", "based", "results",
           "study", "research", "paper", "article", "findings", "data")
corpus_doc <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                              id = "doc", weight = "tfidf",
                              stop_words = stops, min_count = 3L,
                              min_chars = 3L)
head(hg_get(corpus_doc, what = "vocabulary"), 8)
```

```{r corpus-vocabulary-values, include = FALSE}
raw_corpus <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                              id = "doc")
unstopped <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                             id = "doc", stop_words = stops)
n_raw <- nrow(hg_get(raw_corpus, what = "vocabulary"))
n_unstopped <- nrow(hg_get(unstopped, what = "vocabulary"))
n_kept <- nrow(hg_get(corpus_doc, what = "vocabulary"))
```

There are `r format(n_raw, big.mark = ",")` distinct tokens before these
filters and `r format(n_unstopped, big.mark = ",")` after stop-word removal.
The combined count and length thresholds retain
`r format(n_kept, big.mark = ",")`. Keeping the vocabulary filters fixed
helps isolate differences arising from the textual unit used for
hyperedge construction.

```{r corpus-constructions}
corpus_word <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                               id = "doc", nodes = "word", weight = "tfidf",
                               stop_words = stops, min_count = 3L,
                               min_chars = 3L)
corpus_window <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                                 id = "doc", construction = "window",
                                 window = 3, stop_words = stops,
                                 min_count = 3L, min_chars = 3L)
corpus_sentence <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                                   id = "doc", construction = "sentence",
                                   stop_words = stops, min_count = 3L,
                                   min_chars = 3L)
corpus_knn <- text_hypergraph(covid_abstracts, column = "abstract",
                              id = "doc", construction = "knn", k = 10,
                              embeddings = covid_embeddings)
```

```{r corpus-shape-values, include = FALSE}
shape <- function(x) {
  m <- hg_measures(x, what = "summary")
  setNames(m$value, m$measure)
}
s_doc <- shape(corpus_doc)
s_word <- shape(corpus_word)
s_window <- shape(corpus_window)
s_sentence <- shape(corpus_sentence)
s_knn <- shape(corpus_knn)
fmt <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")
```

The summary table records the different dimensions of the five
representations. The document-oriented bag has `r fmt(s_doc[["n_nodes"]])`
nodes and `r fmt(s_doc[["n_hyperedges"]])` word hyperedges, with mean size
`r round(s_doc[["avg_edge_size"]], 1)`. Its dual has
`r fmt(s_word[["n_hyperedges"]])` document hyperedges, with mean size
`r round(s_word[["avg_edge_size"]], 1)`. The window construction has
`r fmt(s_window[["n_hyperedges"]])` distinct sets, and the sentence
construction has `r fmt(s_sentence[["n_hyperedges"]])` segments, with mean
size `r round(s_sentence[["avg_edge_size"]], 1)`. Each kNN hyperedge has
`r round(s_knn[["avg_edge_size"]])` documents.

Among word pairs, pairwise participation is
`r round(100 * s_word[["pairwise_participation"]])`% for document
co-occurrence, `r round(100 * s_sentence[["pairwise_participation"]])`%
for sentence co-occurrence, and
`r round(100 * s_window[["pairwise_participation"]], 1)`% for token-window
co-occurrence. These proportions have different relational definitions
despite sharing the same word nodes.

## Central words under three constructions

For each word-oriented construction, compute clique-motif eigenvector
centrality (Benson 2019). Its adjacency weight is the number of hyperedges
shared by two words. It uses binary membership rather than the numerical
incidence weights. The next tables rank the first ten words under this
definition. In the window representation, identical sets have already
been collapsed, which also affects the interpretation of shared-edge counts.

```{r centrality-bag}
hg_centrality(corpus_word, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique", n = 10)
```

```{r centrality-window}
hg_centrality(corpus_window, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique", n = 10)
```

```{r centrality-sentence}
hg_centrality(corpus_sentence, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique", n = 10)
```

```{r centrality-values, include = FALSE}
top_of <- function(x) {
  hg_centrality(x, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique", n = 10)$node
}
top_bag <- top_of(corpus_word)
top_window <- top_of(corpus_window)
top_sentence <- top_of(corpus_sentence)
shared_all <- Reduce(intersect, list(top_bag, top_window, top_sentence))
only_window <- setdiff(top_window, union(top_bag, top_sentence))
only_bag <- setdiff(top_bag, union(top_window, top_sentence))
window_rank <- hg_centrality(corpus_window, type = "clique",
                             sort_by = "clique")
bag_rank <- hg_centrality(corpus_word, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique")
distance_window <- which(window_rank$node == "distance")
distance_bag <- which(bag_rank$node == "distance")
sentence_rank <- hg_centrality(corpus_sentence, type = "clique",
                               sort_by = "clique")
distance_sentence <- which(sentence_rank$node == "distance")
abstract_text <- tolower(covid_abstracts$abstract)
distance_next <- sub("distance[- ]+", "",
                     unlist(regmatches(abstract_text,
                                       gregexpr("distance[- ]+[a-z]+",
                                                abstract_text))))
n_phrase <- sum(distance_next %in% c("education", "learning"))
```

The three top-ten lists share `r length(shared_all)` words:
`r join_and(shared_all)`. Terms appearing only in the window list include
`r join_and(only_window)`, while terms appearing only in the bag list
include `r join_and(only_bag)`.

The word `distance` ranks `r ordinal(distance_window)` under the window
construction, `r ordinal(distance_sentence)` under the sentence
construction, and `r ordinal(distance_bag)` under the bag construction.
Of its `r length(distance_next)` occurrences,
`r n_phrase` are followed by `education` or `learning` in the processed
token sequences. This provides a concrete example of local co-occurrence
that can affect a window-based ranking. It does not establish that window
centrality is a general measure of phrase importance.

## Groups of documents under two constructions

For document clustering, compare the document-oriented bag with the
embedding kNN hypergraph. Both have documents as nodes. The example uses
the random-walk Laplacian of Hayashi et al. (2020) and requests four
clusters. `seed = 1` makes the k-means initialisation reproducible.
`hg_topic_sizes()` then reports each cluster's document count.

```{r clusters}
bag_groups <- hg_cluster(corpus_doc, k = 4, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
hg_topic_sizes(corpus_doc, bag_groups)
knn_groups <- hg_cluster(corpus_knn, k = 4, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
hg_topic_sizes(corpus_knn, knn_groups)
```

```{r cluster-values, include = FALSE}
bag_sizes <- hg_topic_sizes(corpus_doc, bag_groups)
knn_sizes <- hg_topic_sizes(corpus_knn, knn_groups)
```

Cluster sizes range from `r min(bag_sizes$n)` to `r max(bag_sizes$n)`
for the bag representation and from `r min(knn_sizes$n)` to
`r max(knn_sizes$n)` for kNN. Fixed kNN hyperedge size does not impose
equal cluster sizes. The observed difference in balance is a property
of these fitted partitions, not a general guarantee of either construction.

The kNN object contains document similarities but no word counts.
To describe its clusters, use the same partition with the bag-of-words
hypergraph. Here, `hg_keywords()` ranks words by the sum of their tf-idf
weights across a cluster's documents. The figure shows eight terms per
cluster under this score.

```{r knn-keywords, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9, fig.alt = "The eight words with the largest tf-idf mass in each kNN group"}
knn_keywords <- hg_keywords(corpus_doc, knn_groups, n = 8)
plot(knn_keywords)
```

```{r knn-keywords-values, include = FALSE}
lead_words <- vapply(split(knn_keywords$word, knn_keywords$cluster),
                     \(w) toString(head(w, 4)), character(1L))
```

The leading term in each kNN cluster is
`r paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", names(lead_words), lead_words), collapse = "; ")`.
These terms suggest possible interpretations that should be checked against
the abstracts. The clustering was computed from the supplied embeddings;
its apparent thematic organisation depends on both those embeddings and
the spectral partition.

Apply the same keyword calculation to the bag-based partition so that
the cluster descriptions use a common text representation and score.

```{r bag-keywords}
hg_keywords(corpus_doc, bag_groups, n = 8)
```

`hg_agreement(what = "table")` cross-tabulates the two partitions by
document identifier. The summary also reports label agreement and the
adjusted Rand index. Direct label agreement depends on the cluster labels,
which are arbitrary. The adjusted Rand index compares pairwise grouping
and is invariant to label permutations. It equals one for identical
partitions and can be negative. The `aligned` column sums the largest
overlap with a bag cluster for each kNN cluster. Several kNN clusters can
match the same bag cluster under this descriptive matching.

```{r agreement}
hg_agreement(knn_groups, bag_groups, what = "table")
hg_agreement(knn_groups, bag_groups)
```

```{r agreement-values, include = FALSE}
agree <- hg_agreement(knn_groups, bag_groups)
cross <- hg_agreement(knn_groups, bag_groups, what = "table")
best <- merge(aggregate(n ~ label_x, data = cross, FUN = max), cross)
group_size <- aggregate(n ~ label_x, data = cross, FUN = sum)
names(group_size) <- c("label_x", "size")
best <- merge(best, group_size)
best$share <- best$n / best$size
best <- sort_by(best, ~ share, decreasing = TRUE)
bag_lead <- hg_keywords(corpus_doc, bag_groups, n = 3)
bag_words <- aggregate(word ~ cluster, data = bag_lead, FUN = toString)
knn_lead <- hg_keywords(corpus_doc, knn_groups, n = 3)
knn_words <- aggregate(word ~ cluster, data = knn_lead, FUN = toString)
best <- merge(best, setNames(knn_words, c("label_x", "knn_words")))
best <- merge(best, setNames(bag_words, c("label_y", "bag_words")))
best <- sort_by(best, ~ share, decreasing = TRUE)
matched <- head(best, 2)
cross_words <- merge(cross, setNames(bag_words, c("label_y", "bag_words")))
cross_words <- merge(cross_words, setNames(knn_words, c("label_x", "knn_words")))
clinical_knn <- subset(cross_words, grepl("clinical", knn_words))
clinical_own <- subset(clinical_knn, grepl("clinical", bag_words))
clinical_top <- subset(clinical_knn, n == max(n))
clinical_size <- sum(clinical_knn$n)
clinical_bag <- subset(hg_topic_sizes(corpus_doc, bag_groups),
                       topic == clinical_own$label_y)
```

Under that matching, `r agree$aligned` of the `r agree$n` documents
are aligned, and the adjusted Rand index is `r round(agree$ari, 2)`.
The first two displayed matches contain `r matched$n[1]` of
`r matched$size[1]` documents and `r matched$n[2]` of
`r matched$size[2]` documents, respectively. Their keyword summaries are
`r matched$knn_words[1]` versus `r matched$bag_words[1]`, and
`r matched$knn_words[2]` versus `r matched$bag_words[2]`.

The kNN group described by `r clinical_own$knn_words` overlaps several bag
clusters: `r clinical_own$n` of its `r clinical_size` documents occur in
the group described by `r clinical_own$bag_words`, while
`r clinical_top$n` occur in the group described by
`r clinical_top$bag_words`. Inspect these documents before attributing the
difference to a particular semantic distinction. The table establishes
different assignments, but does not identify a uniquely correct partition.

## Choice of construction

Choose a construction by defining the relation the study intends to
measure. The bag representation measures document-level word occurrence;
token windows measure local co-occurrence after preprocessing; sentence
segments define an intermediate textual unit. The document orientation
supports document-level analysis, and the word orientation supports
word-level measures. Embedding kNN hypergraphs instead measure proximity
under a specified encoder and neighbourhood size.

Report the construction, orientation, preprocessing, incidence weights,
and any window or neighbourhood parameters. Where the conclusions depend
on these choices, compare alternative specifications. An embedding-based
analysis should also consider sensitivity to the encoder.

Journal on Mathematics of Data Science*, 1(2), 293-312.

Berge, C. (1989). *Hypergraphs: Combinatorics of Finite Sets*.
North-Holland.

Ding, K., Wang, J., Li, J., Li, D., & Liu, H. (2020). Be more with less:
Hypergraph attention networks for inductive text classification.
*Proceedings of EMNLP 2020*, 4927-4936.
https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.399

Feng, Y., You, H., Zhang, Z., Ji, R., & Gao, Y. (2019). Hypergraph neural
networks. *Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence*,
33(01), 3558-3565. https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33013558

Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random
